newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's PRD presents alternative economic plan.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's PRD presents alternative economic plan.

text.p: Mexico's main leftist party has unveiled an economic program that calls for a compromise between the statism of the past and current free-market policies that it said were unjustly harsh on the poor.

With an eye on mid-term congressional elections in July, the Party of the Democratic Revolution's (PRD) plan calls for the creation of five million jobs and sustained economic growth fueled by public spending and higher real wages.

The party pledged not to abandon prudence, however, calling for annual inflation of less than 20 percent, budget deficits of less than three percent of gross domestic product and a current account deficit not greater than three percent of GDP.

The PRD's chances of winning a large chunk of seats in the Congressional elections are considered slim. The conservative National Action Party (PAN) is the main opposition force, and it may have an uphill battle to win a majority from the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI).
Still, the PRD's platform was written in the belief that the party would govern Congress for the next three years.

"The PRD's economic program seeks to reduce and eventually eliminate the serious economic impact caused by the brusque transition from one vision of the function of the Mexican state to another," the party's leader, Andres Lopez Obrador, said when the plan was unveiled late Monday.
The PRD's proposals ranged from cutting income tax for small and medium-sized companies, to creating a foreign exchange rate band with a maximum monthly peso slide of 1.5 percent against the dollar.
It also seeks to roll back some of the autonomy of the central bank to ensure monetary policy tallies with government growth goals.
The party said it would raise taxes on capital gains in the stock market and on luxury goods, and would put tax penalties on foreign investment that left Mexico within a year.
On the spending side, it aimed to raise investments in education to international norms, or eight percent of budgeted expenditures, in 10 years, as well as improving health care.

Regarding foreign debt policy, the PRD fell short of repeating longstanding demands for a full-scale renegotiation of Mexico's debt, arguing instead for debt-servicing costs that it said should be maintained at three percent of GDP.
It proposed revisions to the North American Free Trade Agreement linking Canada, Mexico and the United States and the reversal of reforms last year that privatized the pension system.
The party called for a halt to further sales of state-owned enterprises, though it did not advocate the renationalization of those already privatized.
The document stated that "the neoliberalism imposed on Mexicans by the PRI and its governments has not only failed as an economic model, it has also driven millions into unemployment and poverty."
The PRI has governed Mexico for 67 years. It faces tough mid-term elections for Congress in July in which the PRD and PAN are expected to capitalize on the near-collapse of the economy in 1994-95.
More than a million Mexicans were thrown out of work by the crisis, and some analysts say domestic consumption may not return to pre-1994 levels until the next century.
